Context: The Saxon Garden, covering an area of 15.5 ha, was formally a royal garden. There are over 100 different species of trees, and the avenues afford a place for repose. At the east end of the park, the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier is situated. In the nineteenth century, the Krasiński Palace Garden was remodelled by Franciszek Szanior. Within the central area of the park, one may still find old trees dating from that period: the maidenhair tree, the black walnut, the Turkish hazel, and the Caucasian wingnut. With its benches, flower carpets, a pond frequented by ducks, and a playground for children, the Krasiński Palace Garden is a popular strolling destination for the Varsovians. The Monument of the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising is also situated here. The Łazienki Park covers an area of 76 ha. The unique character and history of the park is reflected in its landscape architecture—pavilions, sculptures, bridges, cascades, ponds—and vegetation, consisting of both domestic and foreign species of trees and bushes. What makes this park different from other green spaces in Warsaw is the presence of peacocks and pheasants, which may be seen walking around freely, and royal carps in the pond. The Wilanów Palace Park dates back to the second half of the seventeenth century. It covers an area of 43 ha. Its central French-styled area corresponds to the ancient, baroque forms of the palace. The eastern section of the park, closest to the Palace, is the two-level garden with a terrace facing the pond. The park around the Królikarnia Palace is situated on the old escarpment of the Vistula. The park has lanes running on a few levels deep into the ravines on both sides of the palace.

A number of commemorative events are held annually. On Midsummer's Night, gatherings of thousands upon the banks of the Vistula for a festival called Wianki (Polish for Wreaths) have become a tradition and an annual event in Warsaw's cultural programme. The festival has its origin in a peaceful pagan ritual, wherein maidens would float wreaths of herbs upon the water to foretell the time and manner of their marriage. By the nineteenth century, this tradition had become a festive event, and it is still observed. The city council organises concerts and other events. On each Midsummer's Eve, in addition to the official floating of wreaths, the jumping over fires, and the search for the fern flower, there are musical performances, speeches by dignitaries, fairs, and fireworks by the river bank.

Context: The name of Warsaw in the Polish language is Warszawa, pronounced approximately /vɑːrˈʃɑːvə/ (and formerly spelled Warszewa and Warszowa), which signifies "belonging to Warsz"; Warsz being a shortened form of the masculine Slavic name Warcisław (one may also consult the etymology of Wrocław). Context: There exist, likewise, a considerable number of sites in Warsaw that commemorate its heroic history. Pawiak, the infamous German Gestapo prison, which now houses the Mausoleum of Memory of Martyrdom and a museum, marks but the beginning of a walk through the traces of the Heroic City. The Warsaw Citadel, an impressive fortification from the 19th century, built after the defeat of the November Uprising, served as a place of martyrdom for the Poles. Context: The flora of the city may be regarded as exceedingly rich in species; this richness is principally due to the location of Warsaw within the border region of several great floral regions, which comprise substantial areas that are near to wilderness, such as the natural forests and wetlands along the Vistula, together with arable land, meadows, and forests. Bielany Forest, which lies within the borders of Warsaw, constitutes the remaining portion of the Masovian Primeval Forest; it is connected with the Kampinos Forest and serves as the abode of a rich fauna and flora. Context: The basic unit of territorial division in Poland is a commune (gmina). A city, likewise, is a commune, though possessed of a city charter. Both cities and communes are administered by a mayor; in the communes this officer is styled vogt (wójt in Polish), whereas in the cities the title is burmistrz. Certain larger cities acquire the entitlements—that is to say, the tasks and privileges—which belong to the units of the second level of territorial division, the counties or powiats. An example of such an entitlement is the registration of vehicles: a gmina cannot register cars, this being a powiat's function (that is, a registration number depends upon the powiat in which a car is registered, not the gmina). In this instance one speaks of a city county, or powiat grodzki. Such cities include, for example, Lublin, Kraków, Gdańsk, and Poznań. In Warsaw, the districts possess in addition some of the powiat's entitlements, such as the aforementioned car registration. For instance, the district Wola maintains its own records, and the district Ursynów its own (and vehicles from Wola bear a different type of registration number than those from Ursynów). But in Kraków, the districts do not have entitlements of a powiat; consequently, the registration numbers in Kraków are uniform for all districts.

Context: The Norman dynasty exerted a profound political, cultural, and military influence upon medieval Europe and even the Near East. The Normans were renowned for their martial valour and, in time, for their Christian piety; they became steadfast exponents of Catholic orthodoxy, into which they readily assimilated. They adopted the Gallo-Romance language of the Frankish lands they inhabited, and their dialect came to be known as Norman, Normaund, or Norman French—an important literary tongue. The Duchy of Normandy, which they established by treaty with the French crown, constituted a great fief of medieval France; and under Richard I of Normandy, it was forged into a cohesive and formidable principality in feudal tenure. The Normans are noted both for their culture, such as their unique Romanesque architecture and musical traditions, and for their significant military accomplishments and innovations. Norman adventurers, under Roger II, founded the Kingdom of Sicily after conquering southern Italy from the Saracens and Byzantines, and an expedition on behalf of their duke, William the Conqueror, led to the Norman conquest of England at the Battle of Hastings in 1066. Norman cultural and military influence spread from these new European centres to the Crusader states of the Near East, where their prince Bohemond I founded the Principality of Antioch in the Levant; to Scotland and Wales in Great Britain; to Ireland; and to the coasts of north Africa and the Canary Islands.

Prior to Rollo's advent, the inhabitants of Normandy were not distinct from those of Picardy or the Île-de-France, both regarded as "Frankish". Earlier Viking settlers had begun to arrive in the 880s, yet they were divided into colonies: in the east, in Roumois and Pays de Caux around the low Seine valley, and in the west, in the Cotentin Peninsula; these settlements were separated by traditional pagii, wherein the population remained much the same, with scarcely any foreign settlers. Rollo's contingents, who raided and ultimately settled Normandy and parts of the Atlantic coast, included Danes, Norwegians, Norse–Gaels, Orkney Vikings, possibly Swedes, and Anglo-Danes from the English Danelaw under Norse control.

Context: Robert Guiscard, an other Norman adventurer previously elevated to the dignity of count of Apulia as the result of his military successes, ultimately drove the Byzantines out of southern Italy. Having obtained the consent of pope Gregory VII and acting as his vassal, Robert continued his campaign conquering the Balkan peninsula as a foothold for western feudal lords and the Catholic Church. After allying himself with Croatia and the Catholic cities of Dalmatia, in 1081 he led an army of 30,000 men in 300 ships landing on the southern shores of Albania, capturing Valona, Kanina, Jericho (Orikumi), and reaching Butrint after numerous pillages. They joined the fleet that had previously conquered Corfu and attacked Dyrrachium from land and sea, devastating everything along the way. Under these harsh circumstances, the locals accepted the call of emperor Alexius I Comnenus to join forces with the Byzantines against the Normans. The Albanian forces could not take part in the ensuing battle because it had started before their arrival. Immediately before the battle, the Venetian fleet had secured a victory in the coast surrounding the city. Forced to retreat, Alexius ceded the command to a high Albanian official named Comiscortes in the service of Byzantium. The city's garrison resisted until February 1082, when Dyrrachium was betrayed to the Normans by the Venetian and Amalfitan merchants who had settled there. The Normans were now free to penetrate into the hinterland; they took Ioannina and some minor cities in southwestern Macedonia and Thessaly before appearing at the gates of Thessalonica. Dissension among the high ranks coerced the Normans to retreat to Italy. They lost Dyrrachium, Valona, and Butrint in 1085, after the death of Robert.

The Normans exercised a profound influence upon Irish culture and history following their invasion at Bannow Bay in the year 1169. At first, the Normans preserved a distinct culture and ethnicity; however, with the passage of time, they were absorbed into Irish culture to such a degree that it was remarked they had become "more Irish than the Irish themselves." Both cultures intermixed, each borrowing from the other's language, culture, and outlook. The descendants of the Normans may be recognised by their surnames. Names beginning with Fitz (from the Norman for son) indicate Norman ancestry; these included Fitzgerald, FitzGibbons (Gibbons) dynasty, and Fitzmaurice. Other families bearing such surnames as Barry (de Barra) and De Búrca (Burke) are also of Norman extraction.

Context: In the course of his laboratory labours, Tesla observed singular signals from his receiver, which he concluded might be communications from another planet. He mentioned these observations in a letter to the reporter Julian Hawthorne of the Philadelphia North American on 8 December 1899, and in a December 1900 letter concerning possible discoveries in the new century addressed to the Red Cross Society, wherein he referred to messages "from another world" that read "1... 2... 3...". The reporters treated the matter as a sensational story and rashly concluded that Tesla was hearing signals from Mars. He expanded upon the signals in an article entitled "Talking With Planets" published in Collier's Weekly on 9 February 1901, stating that it had not been immediately apparent to him that he was receiving "intelligently controlled signals" and that the signals might emanate from Mars, Venus, or other planets. Context: Martin Luther was born to Hans Luder (or Ludher, later Luther) and his wife Margarethe (née Lindemann) on 10 November 1483 in Eisleben, Saxony, then part of the Holy Roman Empire. He was baptized as a Catholic the next morning on the feast day of St. Martin of Tours. His family moved to Mansfeld in 1484, where his father was a leaseholder of copper mines and smelters and served as one of four citizen representatives on the local council. The religious scholar Martin Marty describes Luther's mother as a hard-working woman of "trading-class stock and middling means" and notes that Luther's enemies later wrongly described her as a whore and bath attendant. He had several brothers and sisters, and is known to have been close to one of them, Jacob. Hans Luther was ambitious for himself and his family, and he was determined to see Martin, his eldest son, become a lawyer. He sent Martin to Latin schools in Mansfeld, then Magdeburg in 1497, where he attended a school operated by a lay group called the Brethren of the Common Life, and Eisenach in 1498. The three schools focused on the so-called "trivium": grammar, rhetoric, and logic. Luther later compared his education there to purgatory and hell.

Luther, in order to avoid confusing or distressing the people, refrained from extreme change; nor did he wish to replace one controlling system with another. The Eisleben reformer Johannes Agricola contested this compromise, and Luther condemned him for propounding the doctrine that faith is separate from works. The Instruction is a problematic document for those who seek a consistent evolution in Luther's thought and practice.

Certain scholars have maintained that Luther held faith and reason to be antithetical; that is, questions of faith could not be illuminated by reason. He wrote, "All the articles of our Christian faith, which God has revealed to us in His Word, are in presence of reason sheerly impossible, absurd, and false." and "[That] Reason in no way contributes to faith. [...] For reason is the greatest enemy that faith has; it never comes to the aid of spiritual things." Nevertheless, albeit seemingly at variance, he wrote also in the same work that human reason "strives not against faith, when enlightened, but rather furthers and advances it"; this brought claims that he was a fideist into dispute. Contemporary Lutheran scholarship, however, has discerned a different reality in Luther. Luther seeks rather to separate faith and reason, that he may honor the separate spheres of knowledge to which each applies. Bernhard Lohse, for instance, has demonstrated in his classic work "Fides und Ratio" that Luther sought ultimately to unite the two. More recently, Hans-Peter Grosshans has shown that Luther's work on Biblical Criticism stresses the necessity for external coherence in the correct exegetical method. This signifies that, for Luther, it is of greater importance that the Bible accord with the reality outside the scriptures than that it make sense to itself, that is, possess internal coherence. The proper instrument for understanding the world outside the Bible is, for Luther, none other than reason, which for him encompasses the fields of science, philosophy, history, and empirical observation. Here is presented a different picture of Luther, who deeply valued both faith and reason, and held them in dialectical partnership. Luther's concern, thus, in separating them is to honor their distinct epistemological spheres.

Prior to European settlement, the region now comprising Victoria was inhabited by a considerable number of Aboriginal peoples, who were collectively designated the Koori. The first settlement in the area occurred in 1803 at Sullivan Bay, and by 1836 much of what is now Victoria had been included in the Port Phillip District, an administrative division of New South Wales. Victoria was established as a separate colony in 1851, and attained self-government in 1855. The earliest Huguenots to depart from France did so in pursuit of freedom from persecution, finding refuge in Switzerland and the Netherlands. A contingent of these Huguenots constituted part of the French colonists who, in the year 1555, arrived in Brazil with the intention of establishing France Antarctique. A pair of vessels, bearing approximately 500 persons, reached Guanabara Bay, which is at present known as Rio de Janeiro, and settled upon a small island. A fort, designated Fort Coligny, was erected for the purpose of affording them protection against attacks by Portuguese troops and Brazilian Native Americans; this constituted an endeavour to found a French colony in the continent of South America. In the year 1560, the fort was demolished by the Portuguese, who at that time seized a portion of the Huguenots. The Portuguese menaced the captives with death should they refuse to embrace the Catholic faith. The Huguenots of Guanabara, as they are termed at the present time, compiled a declaration of faith for the purpose of articulating their beliefs to the Portuguese; this document, in effect, constituted their sentence of death. This document, known as the Guanabara Confession of Faith, became the earliest Protestant confession of faith in the entirety of the Americas.

Louise de Coligny, daughter of the murdered Huguenot leader Gaspard de Coligny, married William the Silent, leader of the Dutch (Calvinist) revolt against Spanish (Catholic) rule. As both spoke French in daily life, their court church in the Prinsenhof in Delft held services in French. The practice has continued to the present day. The ties between Huguenots and the Dutch Republic's military and political leadership, the House of Orange-Nassau, which existed since the early days of the Dutch Revolt, helped support the many early settlements of Huguenots in the Dutch Republic's colonies. Context: New Rochelle, situated in Westchester county upon the northern shore of Long Island Sound, was the foremost Huguenot settlement in New York. It is recorded that they disembarked upon the peninsula of Davenports Neck, known as "Bauffet's Point", having journeyed from England, where they had earlier sought refuge from religious persecution, four years prior to the revocation of the Edict of Nantes. A tract of six thousand one hundred acres was acquired from John Pell, Lord of Pelham Manor, with the assistance of Jacob Leisler. The settlement was named New Rochelle in honour of La Rochelle, their former stronghold in France. First, a modest wooden church was erected within the community; this was succeeded by a second edifice of stone. Before its construction, hardy men would frequently walk the twenty-three miles from New Rochelle to New York on Saturday evenings, in order to attend the Sunday service. This church was in time superseded by a third, Trinity-St. Paul's Episcopal Church, which houses heirlooms such as the original bell from the French Huguenot Church "Eglise du St. Esperit" on Pine Street in New York City, preserved as a relic in the tower room. The Huguenot cemetery, or "Huguenot Burial Ground", has been acknowledged as a historic burying-ground, serving as the final resting place for many of the Huguenot founders, early settlers, and eminent citizens, with a history extending over three centuries.

Context: It is a logical extension of the compound engine, as previously described, to divide the expansion into a greater number of stages for the purpose of enhancing efficiency. The outcome is the multiple expansion engine. Such engines employ either three or four expansion stages, and are accordingly termed triple and quadruple expansion engines. These engines utilize a series of cylinders of progressively increasing diameter, which are so designed as to apportion the work into equal shares for each expansion stage. As in the case of the double expansion engine, should space be limited, two smaller cylinders may be employed for the low-pressure stage. Multiple expansion engines ordinarily had the cylinders arranged in line, though various other formations were employed. In the latter part of the nineteenth century, the Yarrow-Schlick-Tweedy balancing 'system' was adopted upon certain marine triple expansion engines. Y-S-T engines distributed the low-pressure expansion stages between two cylinders, one situated at each extremity of the engine. This arrangement permitted the crankshaft to be more effectively balanced, thereby yielding a smoother, more responsive engine which operated with diminished vibration. Consequently, the 4-cylinder triple-expansion engine gained favour with large passenger liners, such as the Olympic class, though it was ultimately supplanted by the virtually vibration-free turbine engine.[citation needed]

Context: Lead fusible plugs are sometimes to be found in the crown of the boiler's firebox. Should the water level fall, so that the temperature of the firebox crown rises to any marked degree, the lead will melt and the steam will escape, thereby giving warning to the operators, who may then take steps to suppress the fire. In boilers of all but the smallest size, the escape of steam has little effect upon the dampening of the fire. Moreover, the plugs are too small in area to lower steam pressure to any significant extent, and hence do not depressurize the boiler. These engines exhausted steam into successively larger cylinders to accommodate the higher volumes at reduced pressures, which afforded improved efficiency. Context: The final great advance in the design of the steam engine was the adoption of steam turbines, commencing in the latter part of the nineteenth century. Context: Uniflow engines are devised to remedy the difficulties that arise in the usual counterflow cycle, wherein, during each stroke, the port and the cylinder walls are cooled by the passing exhaust steam, whilst the hotter incoming admission steam wastes some of its energy in restoring the working temperature. The aim of the uniflow is to remedy this defect and improve efficiency by providing an additional port, uncovered by the piston at the end of each stroke, which ensures that the steam flows only in one direction. By this means, the simple-expansion uniflow engine achieves efficiency equivalent to that of classic compound systems, with the added advantage of superior part-load performance, and efficiency comparable to that of turbines for smaller engines below one thousand horsepower. However, the thermal expansion gradient produced by uniflow engines along the cylinder wall gives rise to practical difficulties. [citation needed] The Quasiturbine is a uniflow rotary steam engine wherein steam is taken in at hot areas while exhausting at cold areas.

Uniflow engines endeavour to rectify the difficulties which arise from the common counterflow cycle; in each stroke, the port and cylinder walls are chilled by the passing exhaust steam, whilst the hotter incoming admission steam expends a portion of its energy in restoring the working temperature. The purpose of the uniflow engine is to correct this defect and enhance efficiency by providing an additional port, which is uncovered by the piston at the end of each stroke, thus ensuring that the steam flows in one direction only. By this method, the simple-expansion uniflow engine attains an efficiency equivalent to that of the classic compound systems, with the added advantage of superior performance under partial load, and it is comparable in efficiency to turbines for smaller engines of less than one thousand horsepower. However, the thermal expansion gradient produced by uniflow engines along the cylinder wall gives rise to practical difficulties.[citation needed]. The Quasiturbine constitutes a uniflow rotary steam engine, wherein the steam is admitted in hot regions and exhausted in cold regions.

The oscillating cylinder steam engine constitutes a variant of the simple expansion steam engine which does not demand the use of valves to convey steam into or from the cylinder. In lieu of valves, the entire cylinder oscillates, or rocks, so that one or more apertures therein may be brought into alignment with corresponding holes in a fixed port face or in the pivot mounting, known as the trunnion. Such engines find employment principally in toys and models, on account of their simplicity, though they have likewise been applied in full-sized working engines, particularly upon ships where their compactness is esteemed.[citation needed]

Context: Where CHP is not used, steam turbines in power stations use surface condensers as a cold sink. The condensers are cooled by water flow from oceans, rivers, lakes, and often by cooling towers which evaporate water to provide cooling energy removal. The resulting condensed hot water output from the condenser is then put back into the boiler via a pump. A dry type cooling tower is similar to an automobile radiator and is used in locations where water is costly. Evaporative (wet) cooling towers use the rejected heat to evaporate water; this water is kept separate from the condensate, which circulates in a closed system and returns to the boiler. Such towers often have visible plumes due to the evaporated water condensing into droplets carried up by the warm air. Evaporative cooling towers need less water flow than "once-through" cooling by river or lake water; a 700 megawatt coal-fired power plant may use about 3600 cubic metres of make-up water every hour for evaporative cooling, but would need about twenty times as much if cooled by river water.[citation needed]

A steam turbine is composed of one or more rotors (rotating discs) mounted upon a drive shaft; these alternate with a series of stators (static discs) fixed to the turbine casing. At the outer edge of each rotor, blades are arranged in a propeller-like fashion. Upon these blades the steam impinges, thereby producing rotary motion. The stator comprises a similar, though fixed, series of blades which serve to redirect the steam flow onto the subsequent rotor stage. Often, the steam turbine exhausts into a surface condenser that provides a vacuum. The stages are typically arranged so as to extract the maximum potential work from steam of a given velocity and pressure; hence arises a series of variably sized high- and low-pressure stages. Turbines operate efficiently only at relatively high speed; therefore, they are usually connected to reduction gearing for driving lower speed applications, such as a ship's propeller. In the great majority of large electric generating stations, however, turbines are directly connected to generators without reduction gearing. Typical speeds are 3600 revolutions per minute (RPM) in the United States with 60 Hertz power, and 3000 RPM in Europe and other countries with 50 Hertz systems. In nuclear power applications, the turbines typically run at half these speeds: 1800 RPM and 1500 RPM. A turbine rotor is also only capable of providing power when rotating in one direction; consequently, a reversing stage or gearbox is usually required where power is needed in the opposite direction.[citation needed]

Steam engines commonly employ two independent mechanisms for the prevention of excessive pressure within the boiler; one is subject to adjustment by the operator, while the second serves as an ultimate safeguard. These safety valves traditionally employed a simple lever to restrain a plug valve situated at the top of the boiler. One extremity of the lever bore a weight or spring which held the valve in opposition to the steam pressure. Early valves permitted adjustment by the engine drivers, a practice which led to numerous accidents whenever a driver secured the valve in order to permit greater steam pressure and thereby increased power from the engine. The more recent variety of safety valve utilizes an adjustable spring-loaded mechanism, which is so locked that operators cannot interfere with its adjustment save by the illegal breaking of a seal. This arrangement proves to be considerably safer.

Context: By the late 19th century, it was recognised that air could be liquefied and its components isolated through the processes of compression and cooling. Employing a cascade method, the Swiss chemist and physicist Raoul Pierre Pictet evaporated liquid sulfur dioxide to liquefy carbon dioxide, which, in turn, was evaporated to cool oxygen gas sufficiently for liquefaction. On December 22, 1877, he dispatched a telegram to the French Academy of Sciences in Paris, announcing his discovery of liquid oxygen. Only two days later, the French physicist Louis Paul Cailletet revealed his own method for liquefying molecular oxygen. In both instances, merely a few drops of the liquid were obtained, so that no significant analysis could be performed. The first stable liquefaction of oxygen was achieved on March 29, 1883, by the Polish scientists Zygmunt Wróblewski and Karol Olszewski of Jagiellonian University.

Context: Paleoclimatologists ascertain the ratio of oxygen-18 to oxygen-16 within the shells and skeletons of marine organisms; by this means, they determine the state of the climate millions of years past (see oxygen isotope ratio cycle). Molecules of seawater that contain the lighter isotope, oxygen-16, evaporate somewhat more rapidly than those containing the 12% heavier oxygen-18; this difference becomes more pronounced at lower temperatures. In periods when global temperatures are lower, the snow and rain derived from such evaporated water tend to be richer in oxygen-16, while the residual seawater becomes enriched in oxygen-18. Marine organisms, in consequence, incorporate a greater proportion of oxygen-18 into their skeletons and shells than they would in a warmer climate. Paleoclimatologists likewise measure this ratio directly in the water molecules of ice-core samples, which may be several hundreds of thousands of years in age.

Nearly all ctenophores are predatory, taking prey that ranges from microscopic larvae and rotifers to the adults of small crustaceans; the exceptions are the juveniles of two species, which live as parasites upon the salps on which the adults of their species feed. Under favourable conditions, ctenophores are able to consume ten times their own weight in a day. These variations allow different species to form large populations in the same area, because they specialise in different types of prey, which they capture by as diverse a range of methods as spiders use.

The tentacles of cydippid ctenophores are, as a rule, fringed with tentilla ("little tentacles"); a few genera, however, possess simple tentacles devoid of these sidebranches. Both tentacles and tentilla are densely beset with microscopic colloblasts, by means of which prey is captured through adhesion. Colloblasts are specialised mushroom-shaped cells situated in the epidermis, and comprise three principal components: a domed head furnished with vesicles containing adhesive matter; a stalk which anchors the cell in the lower epidermal layer or in the mesoglea; and a spiral thread that coils about the stalk, being attached to the head and to the root of the stalk. The function of this spiral thread is not wholly ascertained, though it may serve to absorb stress when prey endeavours to escape, thereby preventing the colloblast from being torn asunder. In addition to colloblasts, certain members of the genus Haeckelia, which feed principally upon jellyfish, incorporate the stinging nematocytes of their victims into their own tentacles; similarly, some cnidaria-eating nudibranchs incorporate nematocytes into their bodies for purposes of defence. The tentilla of Euplokamis present a marked distinction from those of other cydippids: they contain striated muscle, a cell type otherwise unknown within the phylum Ctenophora; and whereas the tentilla of all other known ctenophores elongate when relaxed, those of Euplokamis are coiled in that state. Euplokamis' tentilla exhibit three varieties of movement employed in the capture of prey: they may flick out with great rapidity (within 40 to 60 milliseconds); they can wriggle, a behaviour which may lure prey by imitating small planktonic worms; and they coil round the prey. This unique flicking is an uncoiling movement effected by the contraction of the striated muscle. The wriggling motion is produced by smooth muscles, though of a highly specialised type. Coiling around prey is accomplished chiefly by the return of the tentilla to their inactive state, though the coils may be tightened by smooth muscle.

Ctenophores have been compared to spiders in their wide range of techniques from capturing prey – some hang motionless in the water using their tentacles as "webs", some are ambush predators like Salticid jumping spiders, and some dangle a sticky droplet at the end of a fine thread, as bolas spiders do. This variety explains the wide range of body forms in a phylum with rather few species. The two-tentacled "cydippid" Lampea feeds exclusively on salps, close relatives of sea-squirts that form large chain-like floating colonies, and juveniles of Lampea attach themselves like parasites to salps that are too large for them to swallow. Members of the cydippid genus Pleurobrachia and the lobate Bolinopsis often reach high population densities at the same place and time because they specialize in different types of prey: Pleurobrachia's long tentacles mainly capture relatively strong swimmers such as adult copepods, while Bolinopsis generally feeds on smaller, weaker swimmers such as rotifers and mollusc and crustacean larvae.

Context: Ctenophores were formerly regarded as "dead ends" in marine food chains, because it was supposed that their low ratio of organic matter to salt and water rendered them a poor diet for other animals. Context: Homes from the early 20th century line this boulevard in the heart of the historic Alta Vista Tract. The section of Huntington Boulevard between First Street on the west to Cedar Avenue on the east is the home to many large, stately homes. The original development of this area began circa 1910, on 190 acres of what had been an alfalfa field. The Alta Vista Tract, as the land would become known, was mapped by William Stranahan for the Pacific Improvement Corporation, and was officially platted in 1911. The tract's boundaries were Balch Avenue on the south, Cedar Avenue on the east, the rear property line of Platt Avenue (east of Sixth Street) and Platt Avenue (west of Sixth Street) on the north, and First Street on the west. The subdivision was annexed to the City in January 1912, in an election that was the first in which women voted in the community. At the time of its admission to the City, the Alta Vista Tract was uninhabited but landscaped, although the trees had to be watered by tank wagon. In 1914 developers Billings & Meyering acquired the tract, completed street development, provided the last of the necessary municipal improvements including water service, and began marketing the property with fervor. A mere half decade later the tract had 267 homes. This rapid development was no doubt hastened by the Fresno Traction Company right-of-way along Huntington Boulevard, which provided streetcar connections between downtown and the County Hospital.

Context: The Black Death is believed to have had its origin in the arid plains of Central Asia, whence it journeyed along the Silk Road and reached Crimea by 1343. From that point, it was most probably conveyed by Oriental rat fleas which infested the black rats that served as common passengers upon merchant ships. Spreading throughout the Mediterranean and Europe, the pestilence is estimated to have carried off 30–60% of Europe's total population. In the aggregate, the plague diminished the world population from an estimated 450 million to some 350–375 million during the 14th century. The global population as a whole did not return to its pre-plague levels until the 17th century. The disease recurred at intervals in Europe until the 19th century.

Other forms of plague have been implicated by modern scientists. The modern bubonic plague exhibits a mortality rate of 30–75 per cent. and presents symptoms such as fever of 38–41 °C (100–106 °F), headaches, painful aching joints, nausea and vomiting, and a general sense of malaise. If left untreated, of those who contract the bubonic plague, 80 per cent. die within eight days. Pneumonic plague has a mortality rate of 90 to 95 per cent.; its symptoms include fever, cough, and blood-tinged sputum. As the disease progresses, the sputum becomes free-flowing and bright red. Septicemic plague, being the least common of the three forms, shows a mortality rate near 100 per cent.; its symptoms are high fevers and purple skin patches, purpura arising from disseminated intravascular coagulation. In cases of pneumonic, and particularly septicemic plague, the course of the disease is so rapid that there is often no time for the development of the enlarged lymph nodes which were noted as buboes.

Such rock may be subjected to weathering and erosion, after which it is redeposited and lithified to form a sedimentary rock; or, through the agency of heat and pressure, which alter the mineral content and impart a distinctive fabric, it may be transformed into a metamorphic rock. The sedimentary rock may, in turn, be converted into a metamorphic rock by heat and pressure; it may then undergo weathering, erosion, deposition, and lithification, eventually resulting once more in a sedimentary rock. Sedimentary rock is likewise susceptible to re-erosion and redeposition, while metamorphic rock may experience further metamorphism. All three varieties of rock are capable of being re-melted; upon such an event, a fresh magma is produced, from which an igneous rock may crystallize anew.

Context: In the 19th century, shipbuilding and heavy engineering were central to the city's prosperity; and the city was a powerhouse of the Industrial Revolution. This revolution resulted in the urbanization of the city. In 1817 the Maling company, at one time the largest pottery company in the world, moved to the city. The Victorian industrial revolution brought industrial structures that included the 2 1⁄2-mile (4.0 km) Victoria Tunnelling, built in 1842, which provided underground wagon ways to the staithes. On 3 February 1879, Mosley Street in the city, was the first public road in the world to be lit up by the incandescent lightbulb. Newcastle was one of the first cities in the world to be lit up by electric lighting. Innovations in Newcastle and surrounding areas included the development of safety lamps, Stephenson's Rocket, Lord Armstrong's artillery, Be-Ro flour, Joseph Swan's electric light bulbs, and Charles Parsons' invention of the steam turbine, which led to the revolution of marine propulsion and the production of cheap electricity. In 1882, Newcastle became the seat of an Anglican diocese, with St. Nicholas' Church becoming its cathedral.

Newcastle still retains, in many portions of the city, a medieval street layout. Stairs leading from the riverside to the higher parts of the city centre and to the extant Castle Keep, originally recorded in the 14th century, remain intact in several places. Context: The dialect of Newcastle is termed Geordie; it possesses a considerable vocabulary and distinctive word-pronunciations not employed in other regions of the United Kingdom. The Geordie dialect derives in great measure from the tongue spoken by the Anglo-Saxon populations who, having migrated to and conquered the greater part of England following the termination of Roman Imperial rule. This language constituted the forerunner of Modern English; yet, whereas the dialects of other English regions have been greatly modified by the influence of foreign tongues—more especially Latin and Norman French—the Geordie dialect preserves numerous elements of the ancient speech. An illustration of this may be found in the pronunciation of certain words: "dead", "cow", "house", and "strong" are pronounced "deed", "coo", "hoos", and "strang"—precisely as they were articulated in the Anglo-Saxon tongue. Other Geordie words of Anglo-Saxon origin comprise: "larn" (derived from the Anglo-Saxon "laeran", signifying "teach"), "burn" (meaning "stream"), and "gan" (denoting "go").

The Victoria and Albert Museum derives its origin from the Great Exhibition of 1851, in the planning of which Henry Cole, the museum's first director, was concerned. Initially, it was denominated the Museum of Manufactures, opening for the first time in May 1852 at Marlborough House, but by September of that year it had been removed to Somerset House. At this juncture, the collections encompassed both applied art and science. A number of the exhibits from the Exhibition were acquired to form the nucleus of the collection. By February 1854, negotiations were in progress for the transfer of the museum to its present site, and it was renamed the South Kensington Museum. In 1855, the German architect Gottfried Semper, at Cole's request, produced a design for the museum, but this was rejected by the Board of Trade as too costly. The site was occupied by Brompton Park House, which was extended to include the first refreshment rooms, opened in 1857; thus, the museum became the first in the world to provide such a facility.

Context: The interiors of the three refreshment rooms were entrusted to different designers. The Green Dining Room, 1866–68, was the work of Philip Webb and William Morris, and it exhibits Elizabethan influences. The lower part of the walls are panelled in wood, with a band of paintings depicting fruit and the occasional figure; moulded plaster foliage adorns the main part of the wall, and a plaster frieze surrounds the decorated ceiling and the stained-glass windows by Edward Burne-Jones. The Centre Refreshment Room, 1865–77, was designed in a Renaissance style by James Gamble; the walls, and even the Ionic columns, are covered with decorative and moulded ceramic tile; the ceiling consists of elaborate designs on enamelled metal sheets and matching stained-glass windows; the marble fireplace was designed and sculpted by Alfred Stevens, and was removed from Dorchester House prior to that building's demolition in 1929. The Grill Room, 1876–81, was designed by Sir Edward Poynter; the lower part of the walls consist of blue and white tiles with various figures and foliage enclosed by wood panelling; above, there are large tiled scenes with figures depicting the four seasons and the twelve months, these were painted by ladies from the Art School then based in the museum; the windows are also of stained glass, and there is an elaborate cast-iron grill still in place.

Context: The principal front, constructed of red brick and Portland stone, extends for a distance of 720 feet (220 m) along Cromwell Gardens; it was the work of Aston Webb, who secured the commission by winning a competition in 1891 to enlarge the museum. The erection of the building was carried out between 1899 and 1909. In its style it is a curious hybrid, for although much of the detail belongs to the Renaissance period, there are distinct medieval influences at work. The main entrance, comprising a series of shallow arches borne upon slender columns and niches with twin doors separated by a pier, is Romanesque in form yet Classical in its particulars. Among the great treasures of the library is the Codex Forster, comprising several of Leonardo da Vinci's notebooks. This codex consists of three parchment-bound manuscripts—Forster I, Forster II, and Forster III—each of diminutive size, and dated between 1490 and 1505. Their contents encompass a considerable collection of sketches and references to the equestrian sculpture commissioned by Ludovico Sforza, Duke of Milan, to commemorate his father Francesco Sforza. These manuscripts were bequeathed, together with over 18,000 books, to the museum in 1876 by John Forster. Another benefactor of the library was the Reverend Alexander Dyce, who left upwards of 14,000 books to the museum in 1869. Among the volumes he collected are early editions in Greek and Latin of the works of Aeschylus, Aristotle, Homer, Livy, Ovid, Pindar, Sophocles, and Virgil; while more recent authors include Giovanni Boccaccio, Dante, Racine, Rabelais, and Molière.

The collection of glass at the Victoria and Albert Museum spans some 4000 years of the craft, and comprises more than 6000 items drawn from Africa, Britain, Europe, America, and Asia. The most ancient glassware exhibited originates in Ancient Egypt, and the display continues through the Roman, Medieval, and Renaissance periods—encompassing such specialities as Venetian glass and Bohemian glass—and proceeds to more recent epochs, including Art Nouveau works by Louis Comfort Tiffany and Émile Gallé; the Art Deco manner is represented by several pieces from the hand of René Lalique. A great number of crystal chandeliers are exhibited, both English examples, displayed in the British Galleries, and foreign—for instance, a Venetian chandelier attributed to Giuseppe Briati, dated c.1750. The collection of stained glass is held to be among the finest in the world, extending from the medieval period to the modern, and embracing Europe as well as Britain. Several examples of English sixteenth-century heraldic glass are displayed in the British Galleries. Many celebrated designers of stained glass are represented in the collection, including, from the nineteenth century, Dante Gabriel Rossetti, Edward Burne-Jones, and William Morris. There is also an example of the work of Frank Lloyd Wright. Among twentieth-century designers are Harry Clarke, John Piper, Patrick Reyntiens, Veronica Whall, and Brian Clarke.

The collection of sculpture at the V&A constitutes the most comprehensive holding of post-classical European sculpture in the world. Within this collection, there are approximately 22,000 objects, which span the period from about 400 AD to 1914. The collection encompasses, among other periods, Byzantine and Anglo Saxon ivory sculptures, as well as British, French, and Spanish medieval statues and carvings; it includes works from the Renaissance, Baroque, Neo-Classical, Victorian, and Art Nouveau periods. All uses of sculpture are represented, ranging from tomb and memorial to portrait, allegorical, religious, and mythical works; furthermore, statues for gardens, including fountains, and architectural decorations are to be found. Materials employed include marble, alabaster, stone, terracotta, wood (history of wood carving), ivory, gesso, plaster, bronze, lead, and ceramics.

Context: Conservation is charged with the long-term preservation of the collections; it comprises all those held by the V&A and the V&A Museum of Childhood. The conservators are specialists in particular branches of conservation. Among the areas in which conservators operate is "preventive" conservation; this includes the performance of surveys and assessments, as well as the provision of advice on handling items, correct packaging, and mounting and handling procedures during movement and display, all with a view to reducing the risk of damage to objects. Such activities encompass the control of the museum environment—temperature and light, for example—and the prevention of pests, principally insects, from damaging artefacts. The other principal category is "interventive" conservation; it involves cleaning and the reintegration of parts to strengthen fragile objects, to reveal original surface decoration, and to restore shape. Interventive treatment renders an object more stable, as well as more attractive and comprehensible to the observer. It is commonly undertaken upon items destined for public display.

Context: After the defeat of the Khwarezmian Empire in 1220, Genghis Khan gathered his forces in Persia and Armenia to return to the Mongolian steppes. Under the suggestion of Subutai, the Mongol army was split into two forces. Genghis Khan led the main army on a raid through Afghanistan and northern India towards Mongolia, while another 20,000 (two tumen) contingent marched through the Caucasus and into Russia under generals Jebe and Subutai. They pushed deep into Armenia and Azerbaijan. The Mongols destroyed the kingdom of Georgia, sacked the Genoese trade-fortress of Caffa in Crimea and overwintered near the Black Sea. Heading home, Subutai's forces attacked the allied forces of the Cuman–Kipchaks and the poorly coordinated 80,000 Kievan Rus' troops led by Mstislav the Bold of Halych and Mstislav III of Kiev who went out to stop the Mongols' actions in the area. Subutai sent emissaries to the Slavic princes calling for a separate peace, but the emissaries were executed. At the Battle of Kalka River in 1223, Subutai's forces defeated the larger Kievan force. They also may have fought against the neighboring Volga Bulgars. There is no historical record except a short account by the Arab historian Ibn al-Athir, writing in Mosul some 1100 miles away from the event. Various historical secondary sources - Morgan, Chambers, Grousset - state that the Mongols actually defeated the Bulgars, Chambers even going so far as to say that the Bulgars had made up stories to tell the (recently crushed) Russians that they had beaten the Mongols and driven them from their territory. The word pharmacy is derived from its root word pharma, which was a term employed since the fifteenth through the seventeenth centuries. It should be observed, however, that the original Greek roots, from pharmakos, imply sorcery or even poison. In addition to pharma responsibilities, the pharma offered general medical counsel and a range of services that are now performed solely by other specialist practitioners, such as surgery and midwifery. The pharma, as it was commonly referred to, often operated by means of a retail shop which, besides the ingredients for medicines, sold tobacco and patent medicines. Frequently, the place that performed this was called an apothecary, and several languages retain this as the dominant term, though their practices are more akin to a modern pharmacy; in English the term apothecary would today be seen as outdated or only approproriate if herbal remedies were on offer to a large extent. The pharmas also employed many other herbs not enumerated. The Greek word Pharmakeia (Greek: φαρμακεία) derives from pharmakon (φάρμακον), signifying "drug", "medicine" (or "poison").[n 1]

The place of pharmacists in society was expressly defined in the Taihō Code (701) and re-stated in the Yōrō Code (718). Ranked positions in the pre-Heian Imperial court were established; and this organizational structure remained largely intact until the Meiji Restoration (1868). In this stable hierarchy, the pharmacists, and even pharmacist assistants, were assigned status superior to all others in health-related fields such as physicians and acupuncturists. Context: In the Middle East, advances in botany and chemistry were of such consequence that they led medicine in medieval Islam to develop pharmacology to a substantial degree. Muhammad ibn Zakarīya Rāzi, known as Rhazes (865–915), for example, endeavoured to promote the medical applications of chemical compounds; his efforts were among the first of their kind. Abu al-Qasim al-Zahrawi, or Abulcasis (936–1013), pioneered the preparation of medicines through sublimation and distillation, and his work, the Liber servitoris, is of particular interest, as it provides recipes and explains how to prepare the 'simples' from which complex drugs were then compounded. Sabur Ibn Sahl (d. 869) was the first physician to initiate a pharmacopoeia, describing a great variety of drugs and remedies for various ailments. Al-Biruni (973–1050) authored one of the most valuable Islamic works on pharmacology, entitled Kitab al-Saydalah (The Book of Drugs), in which he detailed the properties of drugs and outlined the role of pharmacy, as well as the functions and duties of the pharmacist. Avicenna, too, described no fewer than 700 preparations, including their properties, modes of action, and indications; he devoted a whole volume to simple drugs in his Canon of Medicine. Of great impact were also the works by al-Maridini of Baghdad and Cairo, and Ibn al-Wafid (1008–1074), both of which were printed in Latin more than fifty times, appearing as De Medicinis universalibus et particularibus by 'Mesue' the younger, and the Medicamentis simplicibus by 'Abenguefit'. Peter of Abano (1250–1316) translated and added a supplement to the work of al-Maridini under the title De Veneris. Al-Muwaffaq’s contributions in the field are also pioneering; living in the 10th century, he wrote The Foundations of the True Properties of Remedies, describing, amongst others, arsenious oxide and demonstrating an acquaintance with silicic acid. He made a clear distinction between sodium carbonate and potassium carbonate, and drew attention to the poisonous nature of copper compounds, especially copper vitriol, as well as lead compounds. He also describes the distillation of sea-water for drinking.[verification needed]

Immunology is a science that investigates the structure and function of the immune system; it derives from medicine and early investigations into the causes of immunity to disease. The earliest known reference to immunity occurs during the plague of Athens in 430 BC; Thucydides noted that persons who had recovered from a previous attack of the disease could attend the sick without contracting the illness a second time. In the 18th century, Pierre-Louis Moreau de Maupertuis conducted experiments with scorpion venom and observed that certain dogs and mice were immune to this venom; this and other observations of acquired immunity were later employed by Louis Pasteur in his development of vaccination and his proposed germ theory of disease. Pasteur's theory stood in direct opposition to contemporary theories of disease, such as the miasma theory; it was not until Robert Koch's proofs of 1891, for which he was awarded a Nobel Prize in 1905, that microorganisms were confirmed as the cause of infectious disease. Viruses were established as human pathogens in 1901, with the discovery of the yellow fever virus by Walter Reed.

Non-revolutionary civil disobedience consists in the simple disobedience of laws, upon the ground that they are judged to be "wrong" by an individual conscience, or as part of an endeavour to render certain laws ineffective, to cause their repeal, or to exert pressure in order to obtain one's political wishes upon some other matter. Revolutionary civil disobedience, on the other hand, represents a more active endeavour to overthrow a government or to alter cultural traditions, social customs, religious beliefs, and so forth; for revolution need not be political—that is, a "cultural revolution"—but simply implies sweeping and widespread change within a section of the social fabric. The acts of Gandhi have been described as instances of revolutionary civil disobedience. It has been claimed that the Hungarians, under the leadership of Ferenc Deák, directed revolutionary civil disobedience against the Austrian government. Thoreau, too, wrote of civil disobedience accomplishing a "peaceable revolution." Howard Zinn, Harvey Wheeler, and others have identified the right, as espoused in The Declaration of Independence, to "alter or abolish" an unjust government, to be a principle of civil disobedience.

A great many of the same decisions and principles which apply in other criminal investigations and arrests obtain also in cases of civil disobedience. For instance, the suspect may be required to determine whether or not to grant a consent search of his property, and whether or not to speak with police officers. It is generally agreed within the legal community, and is often believed within the activist community, that a suspect's converse with criminal investigators can serve no useful purpose, and may prove harmful. Nevertheless, some civil disobedients have found it exceedingly difficult to resist responding to the questions of investigators, sometimes on account of a lack of understanding of the legal ramifications, or from a fear of appearing rude. Moreover, some civil disobedients seek to employ the arrest as an opportunity to make an impression upon the officers. Thoreau wrote, "My civil neighbor, the tax-gatherer, is the very man I have to deal with--for it is, after all, with men and not with parchment that I quarrel--and he has voluntarily chosen to be an agent of the government. How shall he ever know well that he is and does as an officer of the government, or as a man, until he is obliged to consider whether he will treat me, his neighbor, for whom he has respect, as a neighbor and well-disposed man, or as a maniac and disturber of the peace, and see if he can get over this obstruction to his neighborliness without a ruder and more impetuous thought or speech corresponding with his action."

Jacksonville is situated within the First Coast region of northeast Florida, being centred upon the banks of the St. Johns River; it lies approximately 25 miles (40 km) south of the Georgia state line and some 340 miles (550 km) north of Miami. The communities known as the Jacksonville Beaches are to be found along the adjacent Atlantic coast. The area was originally inhabited by the Timucua people; in the year 1564, it became the site of the French colony of Fort Caroline, which was among the earliest European settlements in what is now the continental United States. Under British dominion, settlement expanded at the narrow point in the river where cattle were wont to cross; this place was known as Wacca Pilatka to the Seminole and as the Cow Ford to the British. In the year 1822, a year subsequent to the acquisition of Florida by the United States from Spain, a platted town was established at this place; it received the name of Andrew Jackson, the first military governor of the Florida Territory and the seventh President of the United States.

In the year 1763, following the French and Indian War, Spain ceded Florida to the British; the latter soon constructed the King's Road, which connected St. Augustine to Georgia. This road crossed the St. Johns River at a narrow point, known to the Seminole as Wacca Pilatka and to the British as the Cow Ford or Cowford; the names are believed to derive from the practice of driving cattle across the river at that location. The British introduced the cultivation of sugar cane, indigo, and fruits, as well as the export of lumber; as a consequence, the area of northeastern Florida prospered to a greater degree than it had under Spanish rule. In 1783, after its defeat in the American Revolutionary War, Britain ceded control of the territory back to Spain, and the settlement at the Cow Ford continued to increase in size. Following Spain's cession of the Florida Territory to the United States in 1821, American settlers on the north side of the Cow Ford resolved to plan a town, laying out the streets and plats. They soon gave the town the name Jacksonville, in honour of Andrew Jackson. Under the leadership of Isaiah D. Hart, the residents composed a charter for a town government, which received approval from the Florida Legislative Council on February 9, 1832.

During the American Civil War, the city of Jacksonville served as a principal supply point for hogs and cattle, which were shipped from Florida to support the Confederate cause. The city was placed under blockade by Union forces, who seized the neighbouring Fort Clinch. Though no battles were fought within Jacksonville itself, the city was held alternately by Union and Confederate forces on several occasions. The Skirmish of the Brick Church in 1862, situated just beyond Jacksonville, marked the initial Confederate victory in Florida. In February of 1864, Union forces evacuated Jacksonville and engaged a Confederate army at the Battle of Olustee, whereby the Confederates prevailed. The Union forces thereupon retired to Jacksonville and maintained possession of the city for the duration of the conflict. In March 1864, a Confederate cavalry unit encountered a Union expedition, leading to the Battle of Cedar Creek. The warfare and protracted occupation left the city in a state of disruption upon the conclusion of the war.

An instance of this may be seen in employments such as dish-washing or customer service. Conversely, when few able or willing workers exist (low supply) and a great need for their services prevails (high demand), the result is high wages; for competition among employers for employees drives up the wage. Such conditions are found in occupations requiring highly developed skills, rare abilities, or considerable risk. Competition amongst employers tends to elevate wages, for the reason that there is a relative scarcity of workers for the particular position. Professional and labor organizations may limit the supply of workers, thereby causing higher demand and greater incomes for their members. Furthermore, members may secure higher wages by means of collective bargaining, political influence, or corruption.

Context: In accordance with the utilitarian principle, which seeks the greatest good for the greatest number, economic inequality is regarded as a troublesome condition. A dwelling that affords less utility to a millionaire as a summer residence than it would to a homeless family of five constitutes an instance of reduced "distributive efficiency" within society, thereby diminishing the marginal utility of wealth and, consequently, the sum total of personal utility. An additional dollar expended by a poor person is directed to items providing a great deal of utility to that individual, such as basic necessities like food, water, and healthcare; whereas an additional dollar spent by a much wealthier person is very likely to be applied to luxury articles that provide relatively less utility. Hence, the marginal utility of wealth per person ("the additional dollar") diminishes as one becomes richer. From this perspective, for any given amount of wealth in a society, greater equality will yield higher aggregate utility. Certain studies have furnished evidence for this theory, observing that in societies where inequality is less pronounced, population-wide satisfaction and happiness tend to be elevated.

Context: During the 1890s, the University of Chicago, apprehensive lest its ample resources disadvantage smaller institutions by drawing away capable students, affiliated with several regional colleges and universities, among them Des Moines College, Kalamazoo College, Butler University, and Stetson University. In 1896, the university further affiliated with Shimer College of Mount Carroll, Illinois. Under the terms of this affiliation, the schools were required to maintain courses of study comparable to those at the university, to notify the university in advance of any contemplated faculty appointments or dismissals, to make no faculty appointment without the university's approval, and to submit copies of examinations for suggestions. The University of Chicago agreed to confer a degree upon any graduating senior from an affiliated school who achieved a grade of A throughout four years, and upon any other graduate who undertook twelve weeks of additional study at the university. A student or faculty member of an affiliated school was entitled to free tuition at the University of Chicago, and Chicago students were eligible to attend an affiliated school on the same terms and receive credit for their work. The University of Chicago also agreed to supply affiliated schools with books, scientific apparatus, and supplies at cost; special instructors and lecturers without expense save travel expenses; and a copy of every book and journal published by the University of Chicago Press at no charge. The agreement stipulated that either party might terminate the affiliation upon proper notice. Several University of Chicago professors disliked the program, as it involved uncompensated additional labor on their part, and they believed it cheapened the academic reputation of the university. The program passed into history by 1910.

Context: The Yuan dynasty was the first time that non-native Chinese people ruled all of China. In the historiography of Mongolia, it is generally considered to be the continuation of the Mongol Empire. Mongols are widely known to worship the Eternal Heaven, and according to the traditional Mongolian ideology Yuan is considered to be "the beginning of an infinite number of beings, the foundation of peace and happiness, state power, the dream of many peoples, besides it there is nothing great or precious." In traditional historiography of China, on the other hand, the Yuan dynasty is usually considered to be the legitimate dynasty between the Song dynasty and the Ming dynasty. Note, however, Yuan dynasty is traditionally often extended to cover the Mongol Empire before Kublai Khan's formal establishment of the Yuan in 1271, partly because Kublai had his grandfather Genghis Khan placed on the official record as the founder of the dynasty or Taizu (Chinese: 太祖). Despite the traditional historiography as well as the official views (including the government of the Ming dynasty which overthrew the Yuan dynasty), there also exist Chinese people[who?] who did not consider the Yuan dynasty as a legitimate dynasty of China, but rather as a period of foreign domination. The latter believe that Han Chinese were treated as second-class citizens,[citation needed] and that China stagnated economically and scientifically.

Context: The bureaucratic system devised by Kublai Khan mirrored the diverse cultures present within the empire, encompassing those of the Han Chinese, Khitans, Jurchens, Mongols, and Tibetan Buddhists. Although the official terminology of these institutions might suggest a governmental framework almost entirely derived from native Chinese dynasties, the Yuan bureaucracy was, in fact, a composite of elements from various cultures. The Chinese-style components of the bureaucracy were primarily drawn from the native Tang and Song dynasties, as well as the Khitan Liao and Jurchen Jin dynasties. Chinese advisers, such as Liu Bingzhong and Yao Shu, exerted considerable influence upon Kublai's early court, and the central administration of government was established within the first decade of Kublai's reign. This government adopted the traditional Chinese tripartite division of authority among civil, military, and censorial offices, including the Central Secretariat (Zhongshu Sheng) to manage civil affairs, the Privy Council (Chinese: 樞密院) to manage military affairs, and the Censorate to conduct internal surveillance and inspection. The actual functions of both central and local government institutions, however, exhibited a considerable overlap between civil and military jurisdictions, owing to the Mongol traditional reliance upon military institutions and offices as the core of governance. Nevertheless, such a civilian bureaucracy, with the Central Secretariat as the preeminent institution that was (directly or indirectly) responsible for most other governmental agencies (such as the traditional Chinese-style Six Ministries), was created in China. At various times another central government institution called the Department of State Affairs (Shangshu Sheng), which dealt principally with finance, was established (as during the reign of Külüg Khan or Emperor Wuzong), but was usually abandoned shortly afterwards.

Context: The system of government established by Kublai Khan was, in political respects, the outcome of a compromise between Mongolian patrimonial feudalism and the traditional Chinese autocratic-bureaucratic system. Socially, however, the educated Chinese elite were not, in general, accorded the degree of esteem that had been theirs under native Chinese dynasties. Although the traditional Chinese elite were denied their share of power, the Mongols and the Semuren—various allied groups from Central Asia and the western extremity of the empire—remained, for the most part, strangers to mainstream Chinese culture; this dichotomy imparted to the Yuan regime a somewhat pronounced "colonial" colour. The unequal treatment may be attributed to the fear of transferring power to the ethnic Chinese under Mongol rule. Advantages were conferred upon the Mongols and Semuren within the dynasty, and these persisted even after the restoration of the imperial examination in the early 14th century. In general, few North Chinese or Southerners attained the highest posts in government, particularly when compared with the possibility that Persians did so in the Ilkhanate. The Yongle Emperor of the Ming dynasty later remarked upon the discrimination that had existed during the Yuan dynasty. In response to an objection regarding the use of "barbarians" in his government, the Yongle Emperor answered: "... Discrimination was used by the Mongols during the Yuan dynasty, who employed only "Mongols and Tartars" and discarded northern and southern Chinese and this was precisely the cause that brought disaster upon them".

It is the general custom among Kenyans to observe three meals in a day; these are breakfast in the morning (kiamsha kinywa), lunch in the afternoon (chakula cha mchana), and supper in the evening (chakula cha jioni, or known simply as "chajio"). Between these meals, they partake of the 10 o'clock tea (chai ya saa nne) and the 4 pm tea (chai ya saa kumi). Breakfast usually consists of tea or porridge, accompanied by bread, chapati, mahamri, boiled sweet potatoes, or yams. Ugali, prepared with vegetables, sour milk, meat, fish, or any other stew, is consumed by the greater part of the population for lunch or supper; regional variations in these dishes are also to be found.

Cyanobacteria are regarded as the ancestors of the chloroplasts. They are at times denominated blue-green algae, although they are, in fact, prokaryotes. A diverse phylum of bacteria, they are capable of performing photosynthesis; moreover, they are gram-negative, which signifies that they possess two cell membranes. In addition, cyanobacteria contain a peptidoglycan cell wall; this structure is thicker than that found in other gram-negative bacteria and is situated between the two membranes. As in the case of chloroplasts, thylakoids are present within. Upon the thylakoid membranes are located photosynthetic pigments, among them chlorophyll a. Phycobilins, likewise, are common pigments of cyanobacteria; they are usually arranged in hemispherical phycobilisomes attached to the exterior of the thylakoid membranes (phycobilins, however, are not shared with all chloroplasts).

Plastoglobuli (singular plastoglobulus, sometimes spelled plastoglobule(s)) are spherical bodies of lipid and protein, measuring approximately 45–60 nanometres in diameter. These structures are enclosed by a monolayer of lipid. Plastoglobuli occur in all chloroplasts; they become more prevalent under conditions of oxidative stress, or as the chloroplast ages and transitions into a gerontoplast. Under such circumstances, plastoglobuli also exhibit a greater variation in size. They are likewise common in etioplasts, yet diminish in number as the etioplasts mature into chloroplasts.

Context: The evolutionary strategy employed by cicadas of the genus Magicicada utilises prime numbers. These insects spend the greater part of their lives as grubs beneath the ground. Context: The concept of prime number is so important that it has been generalized in different ways in various branches of mathematics. Generally, "prime" indicates minimality or indecomposability, in an appropriate sense. For example, the prime field is the smallest subfield of a field F containing both 0 and 1. It is either Q or the finite field with p elements, whence the name. Often a second, additional meaning is intended by using the word prime, namely that any object can be, essentially uniquely, decomposed into its prime components. For example, in knot theory, a prime knot is a knot that is indecomposable in the sense that it cannot be written as the knot sum of two nontrivial knots. Any knot can be uniquely expressed as a connected sum of prime knots. Prime models and prime 3-manifolds are other examples of this type.

Context: The variant forms of the name Rhine in modern languages are all derived from the Gaulish name Rēnos, which was adapted in Roman-era geography during the first century before Christ as the Greek Ῥῆνος (Rhēnos) and the Latin Rhenus.[note 3] The spelling with Rh- in English Rhine, as well as in German Rhein and French Rhin, is due to the influence of Greek orthography; the vocalisation -i- results from the Proto-Germanic adoption of the Gaulish name as *Rīnaz, transmitted via Old Frankish to yield Old English Rín, Old High German Rīn, and Dutch Rijn (formerly also spelled Rhijn). The diphthong in modern German Rhein, which appears also in Romansh Rein and Rain, is a Central German development of the early modern period; the Alemannic name Rī(n) retains the older vocalism,[note 4] as does Ripuarian Rhing, while Palatine has diphthongized to Rhei and Rhoi. Spanish, like French, adopts the Germanic vocalism Rin-, whereas Italian, Occitan, and Portuguese retain the Latin Ren-.

Context: Within English-language academic treatises, theories respecting imperialism are, for the most part, grounded upon the British experience. The term "Imperialism" was first introduced into the English tongue in its present signification during the late 1870s by those who opposed the allegedly aggressive and ostentatious imperial policies of the British prime Minister, Benjamin Disraeli. It was, shortly thereafter, adopted by supporters of "imperialism" such as Joseph Chamberlain. By some, imperialism was held to designate a policy of idealism and philanthropy; by others, it was alleged to be characterised by political self-interest, and an increasing number associated it with capitalist greed. The Liberal John A. Hobson and the Marxist Vladimir Lenin contributed a more theoretical and macroeconomic connotation to the term. Lenin, in particular, exerted considerable influence upon later Marxist conceptions of imperialism through his work Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism. In his writings, Lenin depicted Imperialism as a natural extension of capitalism that arose from the need of capitalist economies to constantly expand investment, material resources, and manpower in a manner that necessitated colonial expansion. This conception of imperialism as a structural feature of capitalism has been echoed by later Marxist theoreticians. Many theoreticians on the left have proceeded to emphasize the structural or systemic character of "imperialism". Such writers have extended the period associated with the term, so that it now designates not a policy, nor a brief span of decades in the late 19th century, but a world system extending over a span of centuries, frequently tracing back to Christopher Columbus and, in some accounts, to the Crusades. As the application of this term has been extended, its meaning has undergone shifts along five distinct, though often parallel, axes: the moral, the economic, the systemic, the cultural, and the temporal. Those changes reflect, among other shifts in sensibility, an increasing unease, even a fastidious reluctance, with the fact of power, specifically, Western power.

He distinguished between the innate tendency of objects to find their "natural place" (e.g., for heavy bodies to fall), which led to "natural motion", and unnatural or forced motion, which required continued application of a force. This theory, based on the everyday experience of how objects move, such as the constant application of a force needed to keep a cart moving, had conceptual trouble accounting for the behavior of projectiles, such as the flight of arrows. The place where the archer moves the projectile was at the start of the flight, and while the projectile sailed through the air, no discernible efficient cause acts on it. Aristotle was aware of this problem and proposed that the air displaced through the projectile's path carries the projectile to its target. This explanation demands a continuum like air for change of place in general.

For instance, in ascertaining the outcome when two forces are applied to a single object, it becomes necessary to ascertain both the magnitude and the direction of each force in order to calculate the resultant. Should both these items of information be unknown for a given force, the situation remains ambiguous. For example, if one knows that two individuals are exerting pull upon the same rope with known magnitudes of force, yet the direction in which either pulls remains unknown, it is impossible to ascertain what the acceleration of the rope will be. The two individuals might be pulling against one another, as in a tug of war, or they might be pulling in the same direction. In this simple one-dimensional case, without knowledge of the direction of the forces, it is impossible to decide whether the net force arises from adding the two force magnitudes or from subtracting one from the other. The association of forces with vectors avoids such difficulties.

Context: Not only may forces be added together, but they may likewise be resolved into independent components situated at right angles to one another. A horizontal force directed towards the northeast may, therefore, be divided into two forces, one pointing north and the other east. These component forces, when summed by means of vector addition, yield the original force. The resolution of force vectors into components of a given set of basis vectors is often a more mathematically clean method of describing forces than the employment of magnitudes and directions. This is owing to the fact that, in the case of orthogonal components, the components of the vector sum are uniquely determined by the scalar addition of the components of the individual vectors. Orthogonal components are independent of one another, inasmuch as forces acting at ninety degrees to each other exert no effect upon the magnitude or direction of the other. The selection of a set of orthogonal basis vectors is often undertaken with a view to determining which set will render the mathematics most convenient. It is desirable to choose a basis vector that lies in the same direction as one of the forces, since in such a case the force would possess only one non-zero component. Orthogonal force vectors may be three-dimensional, with the third component situated at right-angles to the other two.

Context: The development of fundamental theories for forces proceeded along the lines of unification of disparate ideas. In the 20th century, the development of quantum mechanics led to a modern understanding that the first three fundamental forces (all except gravity) are manifestations of matter (fermions) interacting by exchanging virtual particles called gauge bosons. This standard model of particle physics posits a similarity between the forces and led scientists to predict the unification of the weak and electromagnetic forces in electroweak theory subsequently confirmed by observation. The complete formulation of the standard model predicts an as yet unobserved Higgs mechanism, but observations such as neutrino oscillations indicate that the standard model is incomplete. Context: Since then, and so far, general relativity has been acknowledged as the theory that best explains gravity. In GR, gravitation is not viewed as a force, but rather, objects moving freely in gravitational fields travel under their own inertia in straight lines through curved space-time – defined as the shortest space-time path between two space-time events. From the perspective of the object, all motion occurs as if there were no gravitation whatsoever. It is only when observing the motion in a global sense that the curvature of space-time can be observed and the force is inferred from the object's curved path. Thus, the straight line path in space-time is seen as a curved line in space, and it is called the ballistic trajectory of the object. For example, a basketball thrown from the ground moves in a parabola, as it is in a uniform gravitational field. Its space-time trajectory (when the extra ct dimension is added) is almost a straight line, slightly curved (with the radius of curvature of the order of few light-years). The time derivative of the changing momentum of the object is what we label as "gravitational force".

Context: It is a common error to attribute the stiffness and rigidity of solid matter to the repulsion of like charges under the influence of the electromagnetic force. When the electrons within a material are closely compressed, there exist not a sufficient number of lower-energy quantum states for them all, wherefore certain among them must occupy states of higher energy. It follows that energy is requisite for their compression. Although this effect appears, upon a large scale, as a structural force, it is in truth merely the consequence of there being a finite number of electron states.

Context: It is by ideal strings, which are massless, frictionless, unbreakable, and unstretchable, that tension forces are modelled. Ideal strings transmit tension forces instantaneously in action-reaction pairs; hence, should two objects be connected by an ideal string, any force applied along the string by the first object is accompanied by a force in the opposite direction along the string by the second object. An ideal string transmits tension forces without delay in action-reaction pairs; thus, when two objects are joined by such a string, the force exerted by one along the string is matched by an equal force in the opposite direction from the other. By affixing the same string repeatedly to a single object through the use of movable pulleys, the tension upon a load can be augmented. For every string that bears upon the load, an additional factor of the string's tension acts upon it. Yet, although such machines permit an increase in force, there is a corresponding increase in the length of string that must be drawn in order to move the load. These combined effects lead ultimately to the conservation of mechanical energy, for the work performed upon the load remains unchanged irrespective of the machine's complexity.
